headline: Trump Officials Met Privately With Hedge Funds on Mega Rail Deal
author: Leah Nylen, Crystal Tse, Yiqin Shen and Josh Sisco

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- In a highly unusual gathering, White House officials met privately this week with a group of hedge fund investors betting on whether the $72 billion tie-up between Union Pacific Corp. and Norfolk Southern Corp. will win approval from the Trump administration, according to people familiar with the matter.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The gathering included investors from several major hedge funds and multiple officials from President Donald Trump's administration, and the participants discussed the prospects for the rail deal, said the people, who asked not to be named describing the meeting.

Stakes are high for the proposed merger of Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern, which would create the country's first true transcontinental railroad. The deal requires approval from the Surface Transportation Board, a relatively obscure independent regulator. The Justice Department is expected to weigh in with its views on the merger in the coming weeks. During the second Trump administration the White House has also played a larger role in the antitrust review process.

The investors who attended the meeting specialize in merger arbitrage, a strategy that seeks to profit from the gap between the offer price on an announced deal and the target company's share price. Because merger arbs can make — or lose — large amounts of money depending on the outcome, they pay close attention to the government's regulatory review as they place their bets.
Attendees were invited to the meeting based on their financial relationships with the private-sector organizers, who advertised it to arbitrage traders, said some of the people.

Administration officials didn't share non-public information with the group, according to people familiar with the meeting. Attendees were able to ask officials questions in the private meeting, which wasn't made public by the Trump administration.

In response to questions about the meeting and its attendees, a White House official said in a statement that a junior staffer who no longer works at the White House attended a lunch off the White House complex and that his attendance wasn't authorized by the White House. The STB, which evaluates rail deals, declined to comment.

The $72 billion railway deal has become a major focus for merger arbitrage investors since it was announced last year. As one of the largest transactions pending, it offers the prospect of substantial gains and steep losses, depending on whether traders bet for or against the deal and whether it's completed or falls apart.

The proposed tie-up has also engendered a high-level lobbying push. Trump met in the Oval Office with Union Pacific Chief Executive Officer Jim Vena last year. This summer a coalition of shippers and labor unions sought to persuade Trump's previous chief of staff, Susie Wiles, that the administration should oppose the deal. The battle became even more pitched after the rail regulator forced Union Pacific to publish a video of remarks Vena made in March threatening to raise rates on shippers opposing the deal.
Vena apologized for the comments at an industry conference this week, and said they were meant in jest.
A bipartisan group of senators including New York Democrat Chuck Schumer came out against the deal Wednesday.

The deal's complexity, with multiple layers of regulatory scrutiny and political pressure, gives arbs opportunities to analyze developments and trade around the shifting odds. Hedge funds collectively owned roughly $10 billion worth of Norfolk Southern stock — or about 15% of the total shares outstanding, as of the end of September, according to data compiled by Bloomberg from securities filings.

Merger arbitrage traders closely follow news related to announced deals and attend conferences and public appearances involving key government officials to try and interpret their comments and what they mean for the outcomes of particular deals. They also often hire law firms or consultants to provide insight into how federal agencies or courts might decide in close cases.

Even relative minutiae can be of interest: during the Biden administration, some were focused on the due date of then-FTC Chair Lina Khan's first child and whether it might impact the timing of the agency's decision on Microsoft Corp.'s acquisition of Activision Blizzard.

The DOJ and the Federal Trade Commission, which share antitrust authority to review deals, have for years provided ethics guidance advising senior officials against speaking with arbs outside of public settings. US insider trading laws prohibit government officials from providing material, non-public information to third parties for trading purposes.

Concerns about the rail merger's prospects have intensified in recent weeks. The spread on the rail deal — the gap between the value of Union Pacific's offer and Norfolk Southern's share price — widened to a record of more than $65 a share earlier this week, from roughly $50 a month ago. At current prices, the market is pricing in less than a 50% chance of the deal closing.
"Teach You a Lesson"

Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern announced their plans to merge last year, heralding the tie-up as the first coast-to-coast railway to provide better reach for shippers and move millions of truckloads of goods off congested highways. The agriculture and chemical industries, however, have opposed the deal, arguing it would raise the cost of moving goods across the US.

The DOJ's antitrust division is due to offer preliminary comments on the competitive impact of the transaction by Dec. 3. Those comments are likely to indicate the administration's position on whether the deal should receive a green-light.

The STB, which has sole authority to determine whether railroad mergers are in the public interest, isn't expected to make a final decision until next year. The STB's rules don't just require it to find that a merger doesn't hurt competition; they also require the board to find that a merger would enhance competition in the industry.
While that presents an uphill climb for Union Pacific before the STB, neither the DOJ nor state attorneys general have authority to challenge the combination should it go through.
"We're pleased to see so much participation in the process and value our customers' perspectives," Union Pacific said in a statement.

Union Pacific's Vena touted the benefits of the deal at an industry conference in March, ending his remarks by saying "I'll probably increase everybody's rates that said they didn't want a seamless railroad by three or four extra percent to teach you a lesson."

The company said his remarks were offhand comments and not intended as a threat. The STB, however, ordered Union Pacific to make a copy of his comments available to the public and expressed concern that shippers might be less inclined to offer candid views as part of the proceeding.
"Retaliation, whether perceived or actual, can seriously undermine the integrity" of the agency's review, the board wrote in a Nov. 4 decision.
